title: On Some Versions of Subspace Optimization Methods with Inexact Gradient Information
abstract: It is well-known that accelerated gradient methods possess optimal complexity estimates for the class of convex smooth minimization problems. In many practical situations, it makes sense to work with inexact gradients. However, this can lead to the accumulation of corresponding inexactness in the theoretical estimates of the rate of convergence. We propose some modifications of first-order methods for convex optimization with an inexact gradient based on subspace optimization, such as Nemirovski's Conjugate Gradient method and the Sequential Subspace Optimization method. We study their convergence under different conditions on the inexactness both in the gradient value and in the accuracy of the solution of the subspace optimization subproblems. Besides this, we investigate a generalization of these results to the class of quasar-convex (weakly-quasi-convex) functions.

card.problem: Accelerated first-order methods are complexity-optimal for convex smooth minimization, but many settings provide only an inexact gradient, and standard accelerated schemes accumulate that inexactness in their convergence bounds. Can subspace-optimization methods, which are known not to accumulate gradient error, be given a full complexity account that also charges for solving their low-dimensional subproblems, and can they be extended beyond convexity?
card.setting: Convex smooth minimization with an L-Lipschitz gradient, and its relaxation to gamma-quasar-convex (weakly quasi-convex) functions satisfying a quadratic-growth / Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. The gradient is available only with bounded additive noise of level delta_1; the inner subspace subproblems are solved inexactly to a controlled function-value accuracy. Deterministic analysis; numerical experiments including a non-convex quasar-convex problem.
card.method: Modifications of two subspace-optimization schemes: Nemirovski's conjugate gradient method and Sequential Subspace Optimization (SESOP), each run with an inexact gradient. The inner low-dimensional subproblems are solved by the ellipsoid method or by a multidimensional dichotomy, and the subproblem accuracy is linked explicitly to the inexactness conditions so the total number of (full-dimensional) gradient evaluations, outer plus inner, can be bounded. A restart scheme and a stopping rule handle the quasar-convex case.
card.contribution: Linear convergence of the restarted conjugate gradient method with additive gradient noise for quasar-convex functions under quadratic growth, with a stopping rule trading solution quality against iteration count; a total gradient-call complexity for SESOP and CG when the subproblems are convex, showing the inner solves (ellipsoid / dichotomy) do not materially inflate cost and the schemes stay first-order; and confirmation that neither method accumulates the gradient inexactness, converging to an O(delta_1^2/mu) noise floor.

mathematical_objects.role: The class of algorithms studied and the cost model: complexity is measured in full-dimensional gradient evaluations, and the paper insists its modified schemes remain within this class despite the inner solves.

mathematical_objects.name: Inexact gradient oracle
mathematical_objects.role: The perturbation model; the central question is whether its effect accumulates across iterations, and the answer (it does not, for these methods) is the main qualitative result.

mathematical_objects.name: Subspace optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithmic idea under analysis: minimize the objective over a sequence of low-dimensional affine subspaces spanned by gradients and previous steps.

mathematical_objects.name: Conjugate gradient method
mathematical_objects.role: The second subspace method treated; its convergence proof is generalized to inexact gradients and to the quasar-convex setting with restarts.

mathematical_objects.name: Quasar-convexity
mathematical_objects.role: The non-convex relaxation under which the linear-convergence result is established; the parameter gamma appears directly in the achievable accuracy.

mathematical_objects.name: Quadratic growth condition
mathematical_objects.role: The error-bound-type regularity that, combined with quasar-convexity and restarts, yields linear rather than sublinear convergence.

mathematical_objects.name: Ellipsoid method
mathematical_objects.role: The subroutine for the inner low-dimensional subproblems; its known complexity is what makes the total gradient-call count computable when subproblems are convex.

mathematical_objects.name: Accelerated gradient method
mathematical_objects.role: The complexity benchmark: the paper contrasts its non-accumulating error behavior with accelerated methods that do accumulate inexactness.

limitations: The conjugate-gradient linear-convergence result requires the inexact gradient norm to be sufficiently large at each iteration; the stopping rule is a workaround, not a removal of the assumption.
The total-complexity bound for the inner solves assumes the subspace subproblems are convex; the non-convex subproblem case is not covered.
Solution quality for CG can degrade to O((1/gamma) sqrt(epsilon_0/mu) delta_1), a dependence on the initial residual that the extracted text flags but does not fully resolve.
Only additive gradient inexactness is treated; multiplicative or stochastic noise models are outside the analysis.
Empirical support is a small set of experiments (including one non-convex quasar-convex problem); 'fastest of the compared methods' rests on specific conditioning regimes.

title: The circular law for random band matrices with arbitrary doubly stochastic variance profile
abstract: We consider the convergence of the ESD for non-Hermitian random band matrices with independent entries to the circular law, which is the uniform measure on the unit disk in the center of the complex plane. We assume that the bandwidth of the matrix scales like $n^\gamma$ for some $\gamma\in(0,1]$, where $n$ is the matrix size, and the variance profile of the matrix is only assumed to be doubly stochastic with no additional assumption on its specific mixing properties. We prove that the circular law limit holds either (1) when $\gamma>\frac{5}{6}$ and the entries are independent Gaussians, (2) or when $\gamma>\frac{8}{9}$ and the entries are independent subgaussian random variables. This new threshold improves the previous threshold $\gamma>\frac{32}{33}$ which was only proven for block band matrices and periodic band matrices. After the initial version of this paper, the author further extended the range of circular law for much smaller values of $\gamma$ in 2508.18143 and 2511.01744 when the variance profile has specific mixing properties, but not for an arbitrary doubly stochastic variance profile. Thus the main contribution of this paper is the circular law for a genuine power law bandwidth for any doubly stochastic variance profile. We also prove an extended form of product circular law with a growing number of matrices. Weak delocalization estimates on eigenvectors are also derived. The new technical input is new polynomial lower bounds on some intermediate small singular values, and this estimate does not depend on the specific structure of the variance profile beyond the fact that it is doubly stochastic.

card.problem: Does the empirical spectral distribution of a non-Hermitian random band matrix converge to the circular law when the bandwidth is a genuine power law n^gamma and the variance profile is only assumed doubly stochastic, with no mixing or structural conditions on the profile?
card.setting: n x n non-Hermitian matrices with independent entries; bandwidth scaling like n^gamma for gamma in (0,1]; variance profile doubly stochastic with no further assumption. Circular law proven for Gaussian entries when gamma > 5/6 and for subgaussian entries when gamma > 8/9. Asymptotics n -> infinity.
card.method: Girko Hermitization: control the log-determinant of X - z via the Stieltjes transform of the symmetrized resolvent of a linearized model, plus a convergence-rate estimate for that transform. The key new input is polynomial lower bounds on intermediate small singular values that do not use the profile structure beyond double stochasticity.
card.contribution: Lowers the bandwidth threshold for the circular law from gamma > 32/33 (which was known only for block and periodic band matrices) to gamma > 5/6 (Gaussian) and gamma > 8/9 (subgaussian), for an arbitrary doubly stochastic profile. Also proves an extended product circular law with a growing number of factors and weak eigenvector delocalization estimates.

Threshold gamma > 5/6 is still far from the conjectured regime (gamma > 1/2 or even any positive power).
Subgaussian case is weaker (gamma > 8/9) than the Gaussian case.
Requires the profile to be exactly doubly stochastic; later work by the author handles smaller gamma only under specific mixing properties.

title: Identifiability and Estimation for Unlabeled Finite Mixtures under Marginal Independence
abstract: We study component recovery and mixing-matrix estimation from unlabeled finite mixtures whose observable distributions share the same latent components but have unknown mixing weights. The main identifying signal is marginal independence: each component is assumed to be independent on at least one coordinate pair, but no labels, clean component samples, or mixing weights are observed. We first prove a structural result for product components: under a subset-rank condition on the spans of the univariate marginals, any independent affine combination of the components must coincide with a single component. We then extend this principle to observable mixtures and show that, under the corresponding subset-rank, full-rank, and no-cancellation conditions, marginally independent affine combinations recover the corresponding latent components. When every component is independent on some coordinate pair, all components are identifiable, and the mixing matrix is recoverable under the stated completion conditions. Finally, we propose a Product-Marginal Maximum Mean Discrepancy (PM-MMD) estimator over affine combinations of the observable mixtures and prove uniform convergence and stability under approximate marginal independence. This framework also separates the empirical roles of the assumptions: irreducibility is, in general, not directly testable from the unlabeled mixtures alone, whereas marginal independence yields a candidate-level diagnostic through held-out PM-MMD. Controlled and flow-cytometry experiments show when marginal independence provides a useful recovery signal. In the reported multi-component comparisons, condition-aware representative selection stabilizes PM-MMD and improves recovery relative to clustering, factorization, and pairwise mixture-proportion baselines using the same unlabeled mixtures.

card.problem: When can the latent component distributions, and the mixing matrix, of several unlabeled finite mixtures that share components but have unknown mixing weights be recovered, using only the assumption that each component is independent on at least one coordinate pair?
card.setting: Several observable mixture distributions over the same latent components with unknown weights. No labels, no clean component samples, no known proportions, no parametric component families. Each component assumed marginally independent for at least one pair of coordinates. Both a population identifiability question and a finite-sample estimation question are treated; experiments on synthetic data and flow cytometry.
card.method: Structural identifiability via a subset-rank condition on the spans of the univariate marginals: any fully independent distribution in the affine span of product-form components must coincide with a single component, so the intersection of the affine mixture space with the independence model is discrete. This is extended to coordinate-pair (marginal) independence under no-cancellation and full-rank conditions. Estimation uses a Product-Marginal Maximum Mean Discrepancy criterion (comparing a candidate's bivariate marginal with the product of its one-dimensional marginals via a characteristic kernel), minimized over signed affine combinations of the observable mixtures. Kernel mean embedding deviation bounds give uniform convergence and stability under approximate marginal independence.
card.contribution: Identifiability theorem for mixtures of marginally independent components from unlabeled multi-mixtures, recovering components and (under completion conditions) the mixing matrix; the PM-MMD estimator with proven uniform convergence and stability; a clean separation of the empirical status of the assumptions (marginal independence yields a held-out candidate-level diagnostic, whereas irreducibility is not testable from unlabeled mixtures alone).

mathematical_objects.role: The object being identified: shared latent components combined with unknown per-mixture weight vectors collected in the mixing matrix.

mathematical_objects.name: Marginal independence
mathematical_objects.role: The identifying signal: independence on one coordinate pair per component, strictly weaker than the full independence usually assumed.

mathematical_objects.name: Kernel mean embedding
mathematical_objects.role: Represents each candidate distribution as a Hilbert-space element so that the independence gap is a norm; deviation bounds for empirical embeddings drive the statistical guarantees.

mathematical_objects.name: Maximum Mean Discrepancy
mathematical_objects.role: The discrepancy between a candidate's bivariate marginal and the product of its one-dimensional marginals; its population zero set characterizes the recoverable components.

mathematical_objects.name: Characteristic kernel
mathematical_objects.role: Ensures the MMD is zero exactly when the marginal is a product, making the criterion a valid independence measure.

mathematical_objects.name: Subset-rank and no-cancellation conditions
mathematical_objects.role: Affine-span geometric conditions guaranteeing the independence constraint isolates a single component rather than a spurious combination.

mathematical_objects.name: Uniform concentration of empirical embeddings
mathematical_objects.role: Converts pointwise embedding deviation bounds into uniform control over the whole affine search domain, giving the estimator its convergence rate.

limitations: Each component must be independent on some coordinate pair; components with no such pair are not identifiable by this route.
The no-cancellation condition is essential and is shown empirically to fail badly when violated.
The empirical MMD objective is nonconvex; solvers are heuristic.
Finite-sample analysis of the validation and condition-aware selection steps is left to future work.
Irreducibility is used to complete the mixing matrix but is acknowledged to be untestable from unlabeled mixtures.

title: ProteinZero: Self-Improving Protein Generation via Online Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Protein generative models have shown remarkable promise in protein design, yet their success rates remain constrained by reliance on curated sequence-structure datasets and by misalignment between supervised objectives and real design goals. We present ProteinZero, an online reinforcement learning framework for inverse folding models that enables scalable, automated, and continuous self-improvement with computationally efficient feedback. ProteinZero employs a reward pipeline that combines structural guidance from ESMFold with a novel self-derived ddG predictor, providing stable multi-objective signals while avoiding the prohibitive cost of physics-based methods. To ensure robustness in online RL, we further introduce a novel embedding-level diversity regularizer that mitigates mode collapse and promotes functionally meaningful sequence variation. Within a general RL formulation balancing multi-reward optimization, KL-divergence from a reference model, and diversity regularization, ProteinZero achieves robust improvements across designability, stability, recovery, and diversity. On the CATH-4.3 benchmark, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines including ProteinMPNN, ESM-IF, and InstructPLM, reducing design failure rates by 36-48% and achieving success rates above 90% across diverse folds. Importantly, a complete RL run can be executed on a single 8 X GPU node within three days, including reward computation and data generation. These results indicate that efficient online RL fine-tuning can complement supervised pretraining by allowing protein generative models to evolve continuously from their own outputs and optimize multiple design objectives without labeled data, opening new possibilities for exploring the vast protein design space. Full source code and model checkpoints will be released upon publication.

card.problem: Inverse-folding models (generate an amino-acid sequence that folds to a given backbone) are capped by the small, biased pool of paired sequence-structure data in the PDB and by a mismatch between the supervised training objective (sequence recovery) and real design goals (the sequence must actually be designable, thermodynamically stable, and diverse). How can an inverse-folding model keep improving past its supervised ceiling without new labelled data?
card.setting: Fixed-backbone protein sequence design. A pretrained inverse-folding model is treated as a policy that emits sequences conditioned on a target backbone. Online reinforcement learning with model-generated data and computationally cheap surrogate rewards; no curated preference dataset. Evaluated on the CATH-4.3 benchmark against ProteinMPNN, ESM-IF and InstructPLM, with held-out oracles (ESMFold, AlphaFold3, FoldX, Rosetta). A full run fits on one 8-GPU node in three days.
card.method: Cast fixed-backbone design as an online RL fine-tuning problem. The reward combines (i) a designability signal from ESMFold refolding and (ii) a self-derived stability (ddG) score computed from the inverse-folding model's own backbone-conditioned sequence likelihoods normalized by unconditional priors, avoiding physics-based energy calculations. The objective balances the multi-reward term, a KL-divergence penalty to the pretrained reference policy, and an embedding-space diversity regularizer that penalizes representational collapse. The design space of RL algorithms (GRPO, RAFT, DPO, multi-round DPO), reward compositions, and regularizers is swept to find configurations that are stable across many rounds of self-generated data.
card.contribution: A complete, compute-efficient online RL pipeline for inverse folding that self-improves from its own outputs across many rounds without labelled data, cutting design failure rates 36-48% versus ProteinMPNN / ESM-IF / InstructPLM and exceeding 90% success across diverse folds. Two components are the notable pieces: a ddG surrogate derived from the model's own conditional/unconditional likelihood ratio, and a diversity regularizer acting in protein-embedding space rather than sequence space to prevent mode collapse under online RL.

mathematical_objects.role: The inverse-folding model is the policy; sequences are actions rewarded by surrogate designability/stability signals, and the policy is updated online on its own generations.

mathematical_objects.role: Anchors the fine-tuned policy to the pretrained reference so reward optimization does not destroy the learned sequence prior; one of the three terms in the objective.

mathematical_objects.name: Group Relative Policy Optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The concrete policy-optimization algorithms compared; GRPO-style group- relative advantage estimation is used to turn scalar rewards into updates without a learned value function.

mathematical_objects.name: multi-objective scalarization
mathematical_objects.role: Combines designability, stability and diversity into a single scalar reward so a single policy balances competing design criteria.

aliases: backbone-conditioned likelihood normalized by unconditional prior
mathematical_objects.role: The self-derived ddG / stability estimator: scoring a residue or sequence by log P(sequence | backbone) minus log P(sequence) turns the model's own probabilities into a cheap proxy for folding free-energy difference.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Intro contribution 2: "a self-derived ddG estimator computed from the inverse folding model using backbone-conditioned likelihoods normalized by unconditional priors" — a conditional-over-marginal likelihood ratio, i.e. pointwise mutual information between sequence and structure.

mathematical_objects.name: diversity regularization
mathematical_objects.role: Penalizes low dispersion of generated sequences in protein-embedding space to keep the online-RL policy from collapsing onto a few high-reward modes while preserving functional coherence.

mathematical_objects.name: conditional generative model
mathematical_objects.role: The biological object being optimized: a distribution over amino-acid sequences given a fixed backbone geometry, whose samples must refold to that backbone.

limitations: All evaluation is in silico; success is measured by refolding oracles (ESMFold, AlphaFold3, FoldX, Rosetta), not by experiment, so 'success rates above 90%' means agreement with structure predictors, and reward-hacking of those same predictor families is a live concern despite the held-out-oracle checks.

The ddG surrogate is derived from the very model being trained; using a likelihood ratio from the policy as its own stability reward risks a self-reinforcing bias that the held-out FoldX/Rosetta numbers only partially rule out.

Gains are reported as relative failure-rate reductions on one benchmark (CATH-4.3); absolute designability of the baselines and the distribution of hard cases are needed to judge how much headroom is actually being closed.
The Discussion section was not present in the extracted text (only an empty 'Discussion' heading), so ablation magnitudes, the diversity-regularizer form, and failure analyses are not captured here.
'Continuous self-improvement' is demonstrated over a finite number of rounds within a three-day run; whether improvement saturates, oscillates, or drifts over longer horizons is not established.

title: Gradient descent reliably finds depth- and gate-optimal circuits for generic unitaries
abstract: When the gate set has continuous parameters, synthesizing a unitary operator as a quantum circuit is, in principle, always possible using exact methods. However, efficiently finding depth- and gate-minimal circuits remains a major challenge. The landscape is very different for compiled unitaries, which arise from programming and typically have short circuits, as compared with generic unitaries, which use all parameters and typically require circuits of maximal size. Previous approaches based on random combinatorial search indicate a low success rate even when the circuit ansatz is nominally adequately parameterized, motivating the use of heavily overparameterized circuits. In this work, we present a gradient-based optimization framework that enables the synthesis of depth- and gate-optimal circuits for generic unitaries without overparameterization, even under restricted hardware connectivity. We prescribe parameter-optimal circuit skeletons and eliminate the need for random combinatorial search. We further show that the poor performance of earlier random-search approaches can be attributed to the inadvertent selection of parameter-deficient circuit topologies. By systematically avoiding such skeletons, our approach achieves reliable convergence while maintaining parameter efficiency.

card.problem: Synthesizing an arbitrary unitary as a quantum circuit from a parameterized gate set is always possible in principle, but finding depth- and gate-minimal circuits is hard. Prior parameter-search approaches report low success even when the circuit ansatz is nominally adequately parameterized, and respond by heavily overparameterizing. Why do those searches fail, and can gradient descent reliably hit the optimal-size circuit without overparameterization?
card.setting: Generic n-qubit unitaries, which use all parameters and generically need circuits of maximal size (depth Theta(4^n / n) by parameter counting), as opposed to compiled unitaries that have short circuits. Gate set: arbitrary single-qubit unitaries plus CNOT, possibly under restricted (1D chain or star) hardware connectivity. The synthesis is cast as minimizing the distance between target and realized unitary over the continuous gate parameters. Findings are empirical (hundreds of trials), not proven.
card.method: Fix a circuit "skeleton" of parameterized gates and minimize the target-vs-realized unitary error over the real parameters by gradient descent (GRAPE-style). The key move is a prescription for choosing the skeleton, in particular the CNOT placement, that avoids topologies in which layer symmetries collapse the number of independent parameters and leave the circuit effectively underparameterized. With such skeletons the random combinatorial search over topologies is eliminated.
card.contribution: An empirical demonstration that gradient descent finds depth-, entangling-gate-, and total-gate-optimal circuits for generic unitaries without overparameterization, even under 1D or star connectivity, once the circuit skeleton is chosen by a simple prescription; and the diagnosis that earlier random-search failures are caused by inadvertently selecting parameter-deficient skeletons whose layer symmetries reduce the effective parameter count.

The mechanism (layer symmetries reducing independent parameters) is argued rather than formally characterized; no general criterion is given for when a skeleton is parameter-deficient beyond the specific prescription offered.
Focus is on generic unitaries that need maximal-size circuits; the compiled / structured-unitary case (short circuits) is treated only as contrast, not analyzed.
Only the arbitrary-single-qubit + CNOT gate set is considered; discrete gate sets (Clifford+T) are mentioned only as related context.

title: Leveraging generative hallucination and biophysics-informed modeling for unified biomolecular sequence-structure co-design
abstract: Biomolecular design underpins applications from molecular recognition to therapeutics and synthetic biology, yet de novo interaction design remains challenging-especially for DNA/RNA, underexplored non-protein modalities with scarce, heterogeneous complex data and sharper geometric and chemical constraints. We introduce MCTH (Monte Carlo Tree Hallucination), an inference-only framework that casts all-atom sequence-structure co-design as uncertainty-aware planning over hallucinated states from pretrained folding and inverse-folding models, with optional biophysical control within the same decision loop. MCTH treats these models as frozen black-box operators and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to allocate a fixed inference budget across competing design trajectories, incorporating model confidence and uncertainty, as well as cross-expert consensus/disagreement when multiple predictors are available. Across protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein, and protein-ligand design, matched-budget experiments show that adaptive search improves over simpler sampling and cycling strategies, while held-out AlphaFold3 and Chai-1 evaluations demonstrate transfer beyond the search-time oracle. MCTH provides a shared planning layer across modalities while allowing task-specific folding, inverse-folding, and biophysical modules, requiring no fine-tuning or backpropagation through component models.

card.problem: De novo design of biomolecular interactions (protein-protein, protein-ligand, and especially protein-nucleic-acid and nucleic-acid-nucleic-acid complexes) is hard: sequence and structure are tightly coupled, physics-based energy functions are brittle under local optimization, and learned methods generalize poorly across modalities with scarce complex data. Can pretrained folding and inverse-folding models be coordinated at inference time — with no fine-tuning and no backprop through them — to co-design sequence and structure across modalities?
card.setting: Inference-only, all-atom sequence-structure co-design. Pretrained folding (AlphaFold3-style all-atom diffusion) and modality-specific inverse-folding models are treated as frozen black-box operators; only their outputs (sequences, structures, confidence/feasibility scalars) are used. A fixed inference budget (number of expensive folding calls) is allocated by search. Evaluated on protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein and protein-ligand design under matched compute budgets, with held-out AlphaFold3 and Chai-1 evaluation and a multi-expert variant using Boltz-2 + AlphaFold2 jointly. Evaluation is entirely computational; no wet-lab validation.
card.method: MCTH (Monte Carlo Tree Hallucination): frame co-design as finite-budget planning over hallucinated sequence-structure states. Nodes are candidate sequence-structure states; frozen folding and inverse-folding models propose transitions (hallucinate a structure from an underspecified sequence, redesign the sequence from that structure). Monte Carlo Tree Search runs selection / expansion / simulation / backup to allocate the folding budget across competing design trajectories, with the value signal combining model confidence, predictive uncertainty, cross-expert consensus/disagreement (when multiple predictors are available), and optional biophysical feasibility terms (steric, thermodynamic, energy-like). No component model is fine-tuned or differentiated through.
card.contribution: A single inference-time planning layer, shared across protein-RNA, protein-DNA, protein-protein and protein-ligand design, that turns hallucination-based cycling into adaptive tree search over a fixed folding budget. Under matched budgets it beats fixed-schedule cycling and independent best-of-N sampling, and improvements transfer to held-out predictors (AlphaFold3, Chai-1) not used during search. Integrates biophysical feasibility signals into the same decision loop rather than as post-hoc filtering, and supports multiple folding experts through consensus/disagreement signals.

limitations: Evaluation is entirely in silico; the paper states wet-lab validation is future work, so 'improves over simpler sampling' means improves on predicted-structure metrics, and reward-hacking of the folding oracles is not ruled out despite held-out AlphaFold3/Chai-1 checks.

Matched-budget comparisons are against fixed cycling and best-of-N; there is no comparison to gradient-based hallucination (BindCraft, BoltzDesign) at matched wall-clock, only the argument that those are expensive and initialization-sensitive.

The biophysical feasibility terms are 'optional' and 'energy-like'; the extract does not quantify how much of the gain comes from search versus from adding physics, nor which modalities benefit from which.

Nucleic-acid design is the stated motivation but complex training data for the frozen models is itself scarce and heterogeneous, so the frozen operators may be weak exactly where the method is most needed.
MCTS cost and the branching/rollout design are not visible in the extracted sections; 'fixed inference budget' is compared across methods but the absolute number of folding calls is not given here.

title: Stabilization by rough noise for an epitaxial growth model
abstract: In this article we study a model from epitaxial thin-film growth. It was originally introduced as a phenomenological model of growth in the presence of a Schwoebbel barrier, where diffusing particles on a terrace are not allowed to jump down at the boundary. Nevertheless, we show that the presence of arbitrarily small space-time white noise due to fluctuations in the incoming particles surprisingly eliminates all nonlinear interactions in the model and thus has the potential to stabilize the dynamics and suppress the growth of hills in these models.

card.problem: Does adding arbitrarily small space-time white noise to a phenomenological epitaxial thin-film growth SPDE (with a Schwoebel-barrier nonlinearity) change its qualitative long-time behavior, in particular the linear instability that drives the growth of hills on a flat surface?
card.setting: The SPDE d_t h = -delta * Bilaplacian(h) - div( grad h / (1 + |grad h|^2) ) + sigma * xi on the torus T^d, with xi space-time white noise (derivative of a cylindrical Wiener process), delta and sigma small positive parameters, zero spatial mean, dimensions d = 1, 2. The noise is only slightly too rough for direct fixed-point or Galerkin methods.
card.method: Regularization of the noise followed by a Da Prato-Debussche-type decomposition, with an explicit Fourier-series computation of the stochastic convolution. One shows that the nonlinear current, evaluated on the rough Gaussian solution, degenerates in the limit of vanishing regularization (renormalization, with the counterterms vanishing). The bilaplacian generates an analytic semigroup used for the mild formulation.
card.contribution: Shows that arbitrarily small space-time white noise eliminates all nonlinear interaction in this model: in the vanishing-regularization limit the equation collapses to its linear part, which is stable, so the noise suppresses hill growth. A stabilization-by-noise mechanism driven specifically by the spatial roughness of the noise, in the spirit of the Hairer-Ryser-Weber triviality results for the 2D Allen-Cahn equation.

mathematical_objects.name: Semilinear stochastic PDE
mathematical_objects.role: The object of study; a bilaplacian linear part plus a bounded non-polynomial gradient nonlinearity plus additive white noise.

mathematical_objects.name: Space-time white noise
mathematical_objects.role: The driving noise whose roughness is exactly the feature producing stabilization; its regularity sits just below what direct methods need.

mathematical_objects.name: Stochastic convolution
mathematical_objects.role: The Gaussian solution of the linearized equation, computed explicitly by Fourier series; the nonlinearity is evaluated against it.

mathematical_objects.name: Da Prato-Debussche decomposition
mathematical_objects.role: Splits the solution into the explicit rough Gaussian part and a smoother remainder, and organizes the limiting cancellation of the nonlinear term.

mathematical_objects.name: Analytic semigroup of the bilaplacian
mathematical_objects.role: Provides the smoothing needed for the mild formulation and existence and uniqueness of the regularized solution.

mathematical_objects.name: Gradient-flow energy functional
mathematical_objects.role: Characterizes the deterministic dynamics (attractor of equilibria and heteroclinics) against which the stochastic triviality is contrasted.

limitations: Conclusion section not matched by the extractor; card built from abstract and introduction.
Result is specific to this bounded non-polynomial Schwoebel current; it does not fit the standard polynomial-nonlinearity rough-SPDE framework.
Stated as 'potential to stabilize': the dynamical consequence is argued via triviality of the limit equation rather than a full long-time stochastic analysis.
Requires delta and sigma small; the physically interesting case d = 2 is the hardest.

title: Re-uploading quantum data: a universal function approximator for quantum inputs
abstract: Quantum data re-uploading has proved powerful for classical inputs, where repeatedly encoding features into a small circuit yields universal function approximation. Extending this idea to quantum inputs remains underexplored, as the information contained in a quantum state is not directly accessible in classical form. We propose and analyze a quantum data re-uploading architecture in which a qubit interacts sequentially with fresh copies of an arbitrary input state. The circuit can approximate any bounded continuous function using only one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements. By alternating entangling unitaries with mid-circuit resets of the input register, the architecture realizes a discrete cascade of completely positive and trace-preserving maps, analogous to collision models in open quantum system dynamics. Our framework provides a qubit-efficient and expressive approach to designing quantum machine learning models that operate directly on quantum data.

card.problem: Data re-uploading makes even a single-qubit circuit a universal function approximator for classical inputs by repeatedly encoding features into trainable gates. When the input is a quantum state rather than classical numbers, its "values" are not available to plug into gate parameters. How can quantum data be re-uploaded so that a small circuit still gives a universal approximator of functions of the input state?
card.setting: Quantum machine learning with quantum inputs: the data is an arbitrary (possibly multi-qubit) density matrix, available as multiple fresh copies. The processing register is a single ancilla qubit; readout is single-qubit measurement. Target functions are bounded continuous functions of the input state. Analysis is an expressivity / approximation-theory argument, not an empirical benchmark.
card.method: A sequential architecture: the ancilla qubit is entangled with a fresh copy of the input state via a trainable unitary, the input register is then discarded and reset to a new copy, and the ancilla proceeds unmeasured to the next layer. Alternating trainable entangling unitaries with mid-circuit resets realizes a discrete cascade of completely positive trace-preserving maps on the ancilla, structurally a collision model from open-quantum-system dynamics. Universality is shown by constructing polynomial transformations of the input observables and invoking density of polynomials in the continuous functions.
card.contribution: A quantum-input re-uploading architecture proved to approximate any bounded continuous function of an arbitrary input state using only one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements, with qubit count independent of the number of layers (via reset-and-reuse), and an explicit identification of the construction with a collision-model cascade of CPTP maps.

mathematical_objects.name: Universal function approximation
aliases: density of the model class in C(K)
mathematical_objects.role: The property being established for the architecture; the paper's central claim is that the model class is dense in the bounded continuous functions of the input state.

mathematical_objects.name: Data re-uploading
mathematical_objects.role: The design principle extended from classical to quantum inputs; repeated interaction with fresh copies of the state replaces repeated parameter encoding.

mathematical_objects.name: Completely positive trace-preserving map
mathematical_objects.role: Each layer, after discarding the input register, acts on the ancilla as one CPTP map; the whole circuit is a composition of these, which is the object the expressivity analysis works with.

mathematical_objects.name: Collision model
mathematical_objects.role: The structural analogy: ancilla repeatedly colliding with fresh environment copies; it imports intuition and tools from open-system dynamics into the architecture's analysis.

mathematical_objects.name: Partial trace
mathematical_objects.role: The operation that turns each entangling unitary plus reset into a channel on the ancilla alone; it is what keeps the qubit count from growing with depth.

mathematical_objects.name: Mid-circuit measurement and reset
mathematical_objects.role: Refreshes the input register to a new copy between layers; the mechanism behind the layer-count-independent qubit budget.

mathematical_objects.name: Polynomial approximation
aliases: degree-p polynomial functionals of the density matrix
mathematical_objects.role: The proof route: the architecture is shown to realize polynomial functionals of the input state, which are dense in the continuous functions, giving universality.

limitations: The universality proof is confined to a narrow family of ansatz-agnostic operations (alternating single-qubit rotations and controlled unitaries plus specific polynomial constructions); the conclusion states more general operations are 'largely open'.
Universality is an existence/expressivity statement; no sample-complexity, approximation-rate, or number-of-layers bound as a function of target accuracy is given.
Trainability is only discussed heuristically: the small register 'may' mitigate barren plateaus, but no landscape analysis is provided.
Requires many fresh copies of the input state and reliable mid-circuit reset; the copy cost as a function of accuracy is not quantified in the extracted text.
No demonstration that re-uploading beats a tomography-plus-classical-post-processing pipeline on any concrete task; identified as future work.

title: A Distributed Asynchronous Generalized Momentum Algorithm Without Delay Bounds
abstract: Asynchronous optimization algorithms often require delay bounds to prove their convergence, though these bounds can be difficult to obtain in practice. Therefore, we introduce a novel distributed generalized momentum algorithm that provides fast convergence and allows arbitrary finite delays. It subsumes Nesterov's accelerated gradient algorithm and the heavy ball algorithm, among others. We first develop conditions on the parameters of the algorithm that ensure asymptotic convergence. Then we show its convergence rate is linear in a function of the number of computations and communications that processors perform (in a way that we make precise). Simulations compare this algorithm to gradient descent, heavy ball, and Nesterov's accelerated gradient algorithm with a text classification problem on the 20 newsgroups dataset. Across a range of scenarios with unbounded delays, the generalized momentum algorithm converges with at least 36% fewer iterations than gradient descent, 28% fewer iterations than the heavy ball algorithm, and 16% fewer iterations than Nesterov's accelerated gradient algorithm.

card.problem: Asynchronous distributed optimization algorithms usually need a known bound on communication and computation delays to prove convergence, but such a bound is often unavailable or unknown in practice. Can a momentum-accelerated distributed algorithm be designed to converge under totally asynchronous operation, with arbitrarily long (but finite) delays, while retaining fast convergence?
card.setting: Large-scale convex optimization solved by multiple processors, each updating a block of coordinates and communicating iterates. Totally asynchronous model: arbitrary finite delays between successive computations, between computing and sending, and between sending and receiving. The objective's Hessian is assumed to satisfy a diagonal-dominance condition (known to be necessary for convergence under total asynchrony). Deterministic analysis; simulations on 20-newsgroups text classification.
card.method: A distributed generalized momentum (GM) update that subsumes heavy ball and Nesterov accelerated gradient as parameter choices. Because the GM update is not itself a max-norm contraction, the analysis composes it with itself: the two-step GM map is shown to be an infinity-norm contraction, and the classical asynchronous-convergence theory for contraction mappings (Bertsekas-Tsitsiklis) is then applied to the two-step algorithm. Parameter conditions are derived for asymptotic convergence and for a linear rate.
card.contribution: A distributed momentum algorithm that provably converges under total asynchrony with no delay bound, generalizing heavy ball and Nesterov; explicit parameter conditions for asymptotic convergence; a linear convergence rate expressed in the number of computation-and-communication cycles processors complete, with a characterization of how many operations are needed to reach a given error ball; and simulations showing 16-36% fewer iterations than gradient descent, heavy ball, and Nesterov under unbounded delays.

mathematical_objects.name: Totally asynchronous computation model
mathematical_objects.role: The execution model the algorithm must tolerate; permitting arbitrarily long finite delays is exactly what distinguishes this work from partially asynchronous methods that assume a delay bound.

mathematical_objects.name: Generalized momentum method
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithm introduced; a parameterized update whose special cases are the classical momentum methods and whose parameters are tuned for asynchronous convergence.

mathematical_objects.name: Heavy ball method
mathematical_objects.role: One special case recovered by the GM parameterization and a simulation baseline.

mathematical_objects.name: Nesterov accelerated gradient
mathematical_objects.role: The other momentum method subsumed by GM and used as a baseline; GM is shown to need fewer iterations under unbounded delays.

mathematical_objects.name: Maximum-norm contraction mapping
mathematical_objects.role: The property that drives the convergence proof; total asynchrony converges for maps that are sup-norm contractions, and the paper shows the two-step GM map (not the one-step map) is one.

mathematical_objects.name: Diagonal dominance of the Hessian
mathematical_objects.role: The structural assumption on the objective; some form of it is known to be necessary for convergence under total asynchrony and it is what lets the two-step map be a contraction.

mathematical_objects.name: Linear convergence rate
mathematical_objects.role: The performance guarantee, stated per completed computation-and-communication cycle rather than per global iteration, matching the asynchronous setting.

limitations: Convergence requires a diagonal-dominance condition on the Hessian; strongly convex objectives without this structure are not covered, and the condition can be restrictive for coupled problems.
The contraction property holds only for the two-step (composed) update, not the natural one-step momentum update; the algorithm as run is the two-step variant.
Delays must be finite (though unbounded); the analysis does not address genuinely lost messages or permanently failed processors.
The rate is stated in operation cycles, which makes cross-method iteration-count comparisons less direct; the 16-36% improvement figures come from simulations on a single dataset and task.
Algorithm parameters are fixed a priori by the derived conditions; the conclusion notes online parameter adaptation is only future work.

title: A statistical-mechanical framework for mechanically adaptive cytoskeletal organization
abstract: Living cells continuously remodel their cytoskeleton in response to mechanical cues. Although these responses have been extensively documented, it remains unclear why continuous changes in the mechanical environment give rise to distinct intracellular architectures rather than gradual structural variation. Here, we introduce a statistical-mechanical framework in which alternative cytoskeletal organizations are represented as ensembles of microscopic configurations, allowing configurational entropy to compete with mechanically dependent interaction energies. Rather than reproducing the full molecular complexity of the cytoskeleton, the model asks which features of mechanically adaptive organization emerge from this minimal physical description. The framework predicts three successive structural transitions corresponding to stress fiber formation, alignment, and lateral aggregation. When these transitions are placed on a common cellular-tension axis that increases with substrate stiffness, the predicted sequence is consistent with our measurements of correlation length and anisotropy in senescent fibroblasts. The preservation of this stiffness-dependent sequence despite altered cellular physiology suggests that the observed ordering reflects a robust physical principle rather than a cell-state-specific phenomenon. Together, these results establish a statistical-mechanical framework for understanding how continuous mechanical cues bias the statistical selection of distinct cytoskeletal architectures.

card.problem: Cells remodel their cytoskeleton in response to mechanical cues, but it is unclear why continuous changes in the mechanical environment (substrate stiffness, cellular tension) produce discrete distinct intracellular architectures rather than a smooth continuum of structural variation. What minimal physical principle selects between qualitatively different cytoskeletal organizations?
card.setting: A minimal coarse-grained model rather than a molecularly detailed one. Alternative cytoskeletal organizations are treated as statistical ensembles of microscopic configurations; a single scalar control parameter (cellular tension, taken to increase with substrate stiffness) is varied. Model predictions are compared against measured correlation length and anisotropy in senescent human fibroblasts across a stiffness range. Only the abstract was available for extraction.
card.method: Build a statistical-mechanical model in which the free energy balances configurational entropy of the filament/bundle arrangement against mechanically dependent interaction energies between cytoskeletal elements. Sweep the tension control parameter and locate the parameter values at which the favoured ensemble changes character. The model yields three successive structural transitions identified with stress-fibre formation, stress-fibre alignment, and lateral aggregation of fibres, and predicts how correlation length and orientational anisotropy evolve along the tension axis.
card.contribution: Shows that three qualitatively distinct, experimentally documented cytoskeletal architectures and their stiffness-ordered appearance can emerge from a single minimal free-energy competition between configurational entropy and mechanically tuned interaction energies, without invoking organization-specific molecular machinery. The predicted transition sequence matches measured correlation-length and anisotropy trends in senescent fibroblasts, and its preservation despite altered cell physiology is argued to indicate a robust physical (rather than cell-state-specific) principle.

mathematical_objects.name: canonical ensemble
mathematical_objects.role: Each candidate cytoskeletal organization is represented as an ensemble of microscopic configurations with Boltzmann-weighted statistical selection; this is the framework's core representational move.

mathematical_objects.name: configurational entropy
mathematical_objects.role: The disordering term in the free energy; its competition with interaction energy is what makes the selection between architectures nontrivial.

mathematical_objects.name: free energy minimization
mathematical_objects.role: The selection principle: the realized architecture minimizes energy minus temperature times entropy, so a smooth change in the mechanical energy can move the minimizer discontinuously between ensembles.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "allowing configurational entropy to compete with mechanically dependent interaction energies" — an explicit free-energy trade-off whose minimizer selects the favoured ensemble, though the words "free energy" are not used in the abstract.

mathematical_objects.name: phase transition
mathematical_objects.role: Explains discreteness: as the tension control parameter is swept the favoured ensemble changes character abruptly at three values, giving three distinct architectures rather than a continuum.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "predicts three successive structural transitions corresponding to stress fiber formation, alignment, and lateral aggregation" placed "on a common cellular-tension axis" — discrete changes of the equilibrium state as a control parameter is swept, i.e. transitions in the statistical-mechanics sense.

mathematical_objects.name: nematic order parameter
mathematical_objects.role: The observable that distinguishes the aligned ensemble from the unaligned one and that the model predicts as a function of tension; measured in the fibroblast data as anisotropy.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: the alignment transition and "our measurements of ... anisotropy" — the degree of common filament orientation is an orientational (nematic) order parameter, the natural observable distinguishing the aligned from the unaligned ensemble.

mathematical_objects.name: correlation length
mathematical_objects.role: Observable used to test the model: predicted to grow across the transition sequence and compared directly to fibroblast measurements.

limitations: Only the abstract was available; the form of the interaction energy, the configurational degrees of freedom (lattice vs off-lattice, orientational vs positional), the entropy estimate, and whether the 'transitions' are genuine singularities or smooth crossovers are all unspecified in the extracted text.
The mapping from the model's tension control parameter to substrate stiffness is asserted, not derived; the comparison to experiment rests on this assumed monotone relationship.

Empirical validation is a single cell type (senescent fibroblasts) and two summary statistics (correlation length, anisotropy); the claim of a 'robust physical principle' generalizing across cell states is stronger than one cell line supports.
A minimal model matching a qualitative transition ordering is weak evidence for mechanism — other energy functions could produce the same three-stage sequence.
No quantitative goodness-of-fit, parameter identifiability, or comparison against alternative models is described in the abstract.

title: Error Bound Analysis for the Regularized Loss of Deep Linear Neural Networks
abstract: The optimization foundations of deep linear networks have recently received significant attention. However, due to their inherent non-convexity and hierarchical structure, analyzing the loss functions of deep linear networks remains a challenging task. In this work, we study the local geometry of the regularized squared loss of deep linear networks around each critical point. Specifically, we obtain a closed-form characterization of the critical point set building on existing results and establish an error bound for the regularized loss under mild conditions on network width and regularization parameters. Notably, this error bound quantifies the distance from a point to the critical point set in terms of the current gradient norm, which can be used to derive linear convergence of first-order methods. To support our theoretical findings, we conduct numerical experiments and demonstrate that gradient descent converges linearly to a critical point when optimizing the regularized loss of deep linear networks.

card.problem: The regularized squared loss of a deep linear network is non-convex with a hierarchical product structure, and existing convergence analyses of gradient descent are tied to specific initializations and only cover convergence to global minima. Can the local geometry around every critical point (global min, local min, or saddle) be characterized well enough to conclude linear convergence of first-order methods regardless of which critical point is approached?
card.setting: Objective is ||W_L ... W_1 - Y||_F^2 plus a sum of Frobenius-norm penalties lambda_l ||W_l||_F^2, with L >= 2 layers, arbitrary target matrix Y, and each hidden width at least as large as the input and output widths (an explicit assumption). Mild conditions on the regularization parameters. Deterministic full-batch analysis of local geometry; numerical experiments with gradient descent.
card.method: Specialize an existing closed-form characterization of the critical-point set of the regularized deep linear loss under the width assumption, obtaining an explicit description of that set. Then prove that near every critical point the distance to the critical-point set is bounded by a constant times the gradient norm (a local error bound / Lojasiewicz-type inequality with exponent 1/2). Feed this into the standard error-bound-implies-linear-convergence framework for smooth non-convex problems.
card.contribution: A closed-form characterization of the critical-point set of the regularized deep linear loss for networks of arbitrary depth (previous results covered two layers and only global minima), and a proof that this loss satisfies a local error bound at every critical point under mild width and regularization conditions. The error bound quantifies distance to the critical set by the current gradient norm and hence implies linear convergence of gradient descent to a critical point, matched by experiments.

mathematical_objects.role: The model whose loss landscape is analyzed; the product W_L...W_1 is the source of non-convexity and the hierarchical structure the analysis must handle.

mathematical_objects.name: Regularized squared loss
mathematical_objects.role: The specific objective; adding the Frobenius penalties is what makes existing unregularized-network analyses inapplicable and what the paper's geometry is about.

mathematical_objects.name: Error bound condition
mathematical_objects.role: The regularity property proved: distance to the critical set is controlled by the gradient norm; it is the hinge from which linear convergence follows.

mathematical_objects.name: Critical point set
mathematical_objects.role: The target set for the error bound; the paper first derives its closed form, then measures approach to it. Includes saddles and local minima, not just global.

mathematical_objects.name: Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality
mathematical_objects.role: Cited as equivalent to the error bound under mild conditions and as the more familiar route to linear convergence of gradient descent on non-convex losses.

mathematical_objects.name: Gradient descent
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithm whose linear convergence to a critical point is the payoff of the error bound and is verified numerically.

mathematical_objects.name: Balancedness / approximate balancedness of weights
mathematical_objects.role: Structural condition on layerwise weights used in prior deep-linear analyses; the extracted text positions this work as avoiding the carefully-designed initialization those analyses need.

limitations: No conclusion section was extracted; the exact statement of the error bound (the constant kappa, the neighborhood radius epsilon, the precise 'mild conditions' on widths and regularization) could not be verified from the source. Card at low confidence per curator protocol.
Linearity of the network is essential; the analysis does not extend to nonlinear activations, and the extracted text does not claim it does.
The result guarantees linear convergence to some critical point, which may be a saddle or a poor local minimum; it says nothing about which critical point GD reaches or about solution quality.
Requires every hidden layer to be at least as wide as the input and output layers; bottleneck architectures are excluded.
Empirical validation is limited to demonstrating linear convergence of GD on the regularized loss, not comparison against alternative analyses or optimizers.

title: Duality of causal distributionally robust optimization
abstract: We study distributionally robust optimization (DRO) in a dynamic context, where model uncertainty is captured by penalizing potential models based on their adapted Wasserstein distance to a reference model. We consider both discrete- and continuous-time settings and derive dynamic duality formulas that reformulate the worst-case expectation as a tractable minimax problem. The inner maximization admits a recursive representation in discrete time, while in continuous time, it is characterized by a path-dependent Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation. We further extend these duality results from the worst-case expectation to the worst-case expected shortfall, a non-linear expectation. Finally, we apply this framework to optimal stopping problems in discrete time. We recast the original problem as a classical Wasserstein DRO on a nested space by introducing a novel relaxation that considers stopping times with respect to general filtrations.

card.problem: Can distributionally robust optimization be made tractable in a dynamic (multi-period / continuous-time) setting when the ambiguity set is a causal or adapted Wasserstein ball around a reference model rather than a standard Wasserstein ball?
card.setting: Stochastic processes in discrete and continuous time on a filtered space. Model uncertainty penalized by the causal or bicausal (adapted) Wasserstein distance, or a penalized variant. Objectives: worst-case linear expectation, worst-case expected shortfall (a concave nonlinear expectation), and worst-case value of an optimal stopping problem (in general not concave), the last in discrete time.
card.method: Convex / Lagrangian duality converting the penalized worst-case problem into inf over lambda >= 0 of L*(lambda) + U(lambda), where L* is the convex conjugate of the penalty and U is a convex function given by a dynamic programming principle. U is computed by a recursion in discrete time and by a path-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, derived via functional Ito calculus, in continuous time. Optimal stopping is handled by a concave relaxation lifting the problem to the space of adapted processes on a nested space, recasting it as a classical Wasserstein DRO.
card.contribution: First dynamic duality for causal DRO in continuous time; extension from worst-case expectation to worst-case expected shortfall (a nonlinear expectation); a relaxation recasting causal distributionally robust optimal stopping as Wasserstein DRO on a nested space; a proof that causal and bicausal penalizations are equivalent under mild conditions; a demonstration that the causal constraint shrinks the ambiguity set and reduces over-conservatism relative to standard Wasserstein DRO in dynamic problems.

mathematical_objects.name: Adapted Wasserstein distance
mathematical_objects.role: Defines the ambiguity set; it penalizes differences in the information flow of models, not only their spatial distance, which is what makes the dynamic problem well posed.

mathematical_objects.name: Causal optimal transport
mathematical_objects.role: The transport problem whose cost defines the ambiguity radius; its computational hardness is the obstacle the duality circumvents.

mathematical_objects.name: Distributionally robust optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The minimax framework being lifted to a dynamic setting.

mathematical_objects.name: Convex conjugate / Fenchel duality
mathematical_objects.role: Turns the penalized worst-case expectation into a one-dimensional minimization over the Lagrange multiplier lambda.

mathematical_objects.name: Path-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation
mathematical_objects.role: Characterizes the inner value function U in continuous time, obtained by treating the dual as a non-Markovian stochastic control problem.

mathematical_objects.name: Functional Ito calculus
mathematical_objects.role: Supplies the horizontal and vertical derivatives needed to write the path-dependent HJB equation.

mathematical_objects.name: Expected shortfall
mathematical_objects.role: The concave nonlinear objective functional to which the duality is extended beyond the linear expectation case.

mathematical_objects.name: Optimal stopping
mathematical_objects.role: The non-concave objective handled by the concave relaxation on the nested space of adapted processes.

Continuous-time results need regularity conditions and the functional Ito framework.
The optimal stopping treatment is restricted to discrete time.
Value functions of optimal stopping are discontinuous in the standard Wasserstein topology, which motivates but also confines the causal approach.

title: Resolvent convergence for sample second-moment matrices with heterogeneous profile
abstract: We study the resolvent \(G^z=\left(\frac{1}{n}XX^{\top}-zI_p\right)^{-1}\), where \(z\in\mathbb{C}\) satisfies \(\Im(z)>0\) and \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\) is a random matrix with independent, but not necessarily identically distributed, columns. The columns are real-valued and have finite second moments, but need not be centered. We identify a deterministic equivalent \(\tilde G^z\) through a finite-dimensional fixed-point system depending on the full second-moment profile \((\mathbb{E}[x_ix_i^{\top}])_{i\in[n]}\). Our quantitative, dimension-dependent bounds are expressed in terms of moments of the centered quadratic forms \(q_i(A):=x_i^{\top}Ax_i-\mathbb{E}[x_i^{\top}Ax_i]\), normalized either by the Hilbert--Schmidt norm or by the operator norm of \(A\). In particular, no independence between the entries of a given column is required. We prove quantitative comparison bounds between \(\operatorname{tr}(BG^z)\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(B\tilde G^z)\) in several regimes. We first consider heterogeneous profiles with uniformly bounded operator norm and bounded aspect ratio. Sharper, profile-adapted arguments then cover uniformly bounded Hilbert--Schmidt second moments without any aspect-ratio condition, a common profile for which additional operator-norm estimates are obtained, and profiles taking \(k\) pairwise commuting values, for which the Hilbert--Schmidt bounds incur a linear loss in \(k\). All probabilistic estimates are global for a fixed \(z\in\mathbb{H}\); the regime \(\Im(z)\downarrow0\) is not considered. The Hilbert--Schmidt estimate yields an explicit random-to-deterministic convergence rate and recovers the Marchenko--Pastur limit in the centered i.i.d. setting under the existence of a moment strictly larger than two.

card.problem: Can quantitative deterministic equivalents for the resolvent of the uncentered sample second-moment matrix (1/n) X X^T be established when the columns are independent but not identically distributed, possibly non-centered, and with arbitrary dependence among the coordinates of each column?
card.setting: X in R^{p x n} with independent columns x_i, finite second moment Sigma_i = E[x_i x_i^T], no i.i.d. assumption, no centering, no entrywise independence within a column. Spectral parameter z fixed in the open upper half plane; the regime Im z -> 0 is not treated. Bounds are dimension-explicit and hold in L^q. Assumptions enter only through moments of centered quadratic forms.
card.method: A finite-profile self-consistent fixed-point system extending the Marchenko-Pastur scalar equation. A deterministic module proves existence, uniqueness, Stieltjes-transform structure, compact support and stability of the profile equation. A probabilistic module uses resolvent replacement, leave-one-out identities and L^q moments of centered quadratic forms x_i^T B x_i - tr(Sigma_i B), normalized by either the Hilbert-Schmidt or the operator norm of the test matrix.
card.contribution: Quantitative comparison bounds for tr(A(G^z - G-tilde^z)) under weak quadratic-form control only: no subgaussian assumption, no global concentration property, no independence among column coordinates, no limiting profile distribution, no common covariance. Profile-adapted estimates distinguish the Hilbert-Schmidt and operator test geometries; a k commuting-values profile incurs only linear-in-k loss; the centered i.i.d. case recovers Marchenko-Pastur with an explicit rate under any moment strictly above two.
