mathematical_objects.role: The deterministic matrix G-tilde^z approximating the random resolvent; the whole paper is about validating it quantitatively under weak hypotheses.

mathematical_objects.name: Self-consistent equation
mathematical_objects.role: The finite family of coupled equations defining the deterministic equivalent; its stability estimate transfers random fluctuations into deterministic error.

mathematical_objects.name: Marchenko-Pastur law
mathematical_objects.role: The scalar limit the profile equation generalizes and the benchmark recovered in the centered i.i.d. special case.

mathematical_objects.name: Centered quadratic forms
mathematical_objects.role: The sole channel through which model assumptions enter; their L^q moments, normalized by Hilbert-Schmidt or operator norm, index all the bounds.

mathematical_objects.name: Leave-one-out / resolvent perturbation identities
mathematical_objects.role: Decompose the resolvent column by column so that each increment is governed by one quadratic form.

mathematical_objects.name: Stieltjes transform
mathematical_objects.role: Encodes the empirical spectral distribution and gives the deterministic equivalent the analytic structure (Nevanlinna / real-measure) used for existence and support control.

mathematical_objects.name: Second-moment profile
mathematical_objects.role: The unrestricted family (Sigma_i) that parametrizes the model; the point is that no structural condition (diagonalizability, isotropy, convergence) is placed on it.

limitations: Conclusion section not matched by the extractor; card built from abstract and introduction.
Estimates hold only at fixed z in the upper half plane; these are not local laws and say nothing about the spectral edge or the real axis.
The k commuting-values bound loses a factor linear in k.
No analysis of mean-induced outliers or of separating a deterministic mean from centered noise.

title: Quantum Markovian Dynamics from a Double Covariance Stochastic Framework
abstract: We develop an interacting extension of the Double Covariance Model (DCM), a stochastic subquantum framework in which macroscopic quantum dynamics emerge through coarse-graining of correlated microscopic fluctuations. Starting from local stochastic differential equations on subsystem Hilbert spaces, we derive a closed evolution equation for a coarse-grained double covariance operator using multi-scale It\^o calculus and sliding-window averaging. The construction explicitly incorporates two separated temporal scales: a fast microscopic fluctuation scale governing subquantum stochastic processes and a slower macroscopic observation scale associated with coarse-grained dynamics. Within the hydrodynamic limit, where the ratio between microscopic correlation time and averaging-window scale vanishes, rapidly fluctuating corrections disappear and the effective dynamics converges to a deterministic macroscopic transport equation. We show that the emergent macroscopic dynamics has the exact Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) form: coherent Hamiltonian evolution arises from deterministic subquantum flow, while dissipative channels emerge from quadratic noise correlations. The framework further demonstrates how non-separable interaction Hamiltonians can arise from strictly local, state-dependent stochastic feedback fields. In the fluctuation-free limit, the model reduces naturally to the standard von Neumann equation, providing a unified stochastic foundation for both open and closed quantum dynamics.

card.problem: Can the standard evolution equations of quantum theory (the Lindblad master equation for open systems, the von Neumann equation for closed systems) be derived from classical correlated stochastic processes on subsystem Hilbert spaces via coarse-graining, rather than postulated?
card.setting: Local Ito stochastic differential equations on subsystem Hilbert spaces. Two separated time scales: a fast microscopic fluctuation scale with correlation time of order epsilon^2 and a slower macroscopic averaging window of order epsilon. The macroscopic dynamics is obtained in the hydrodynamic limit epsilon -> 0. Interacting composite systems are modeled by local, state-dependent stochastic feedback fields.
card.method: Multi-scale Ito calculus combined with sliding-window time averaging to derive a closed evolution equation for a coarse-grained double covariance operator (a fourth-order statistical object: covariance of microscopic time-window correlations). A homogenization / hydrodynamic limit removes the fast fluctuations; the deterministic drift yields the Hamiltonian commutator and the quadratic-variation (noise covariance) terms yield the dissipative channels.
card.contribution: Shows the normalized double covariance obeys exactly the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad equation, with unitary von Neumann evolution recovered as the fluctuation-free limit; demonstrates that non-separable interaction Hamiltonians can emerge from strictly local state-dependent stochastic feedback; provides a single classical-stochastic foundation for both open and closed quantum dynamics, in contrast to noncommutative quantum stochastic calculus.

mathematical_objects.name: Ito stochastic differential equation
mathematical_objects.role: The microscopic law for the subquantum processes on each subsystem Hilbert space; the starting point of the construction.

mathematical_objects.name: Quadratic variation
mathematical_objects.role: The bracket terms that, after coarse-graining, become the dissipative (Lindblad) part of the macroscopic generator.

mathematical_objects.name: Multi-scale homogenization limit
mathematical_objects.role: Sends the ratio of microscopic correlation time to averaging window to zero, killing fast fluctuations and leaving a deterministic transport equation.

mathematical_objects.name: GKSL generator
mathematical_objects.role: The target macroscopic equation shown to emerge exactly from the two-scale stochastic dynamics.

mathematical_objects.name: Covariance operator
mathematical_objects.role: The coarse-grained state object that plays the role of the density operator and whose evolution equation is derived.

mathematical_objects.name: Sliding-window time averaging
mathematical_objects.role: The coarse-graining operation that separates macroscopic observables from microscopic fluctuations.

limitations: Conclusion is very brief; the paper is a physics reconstruction program and the rigor of the epsilon -> 0 limit is relegated to an appendix, not assessable from the extract.
Relies on the specific scaling (window of order epsilon, correlation time of order epsilon^2).
The subquantum interpretation is model-specific; portability rests on the averaging argument, not the physical framing.
Confidence low: statistical-physics-adjacent, limited visible rigor.

title: Task- and dataset-specific information in protein language models
abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have transferred the latest advances from natural language processing to computational biology. These models, trained on large corpora of protein sequence data, are widely used to translate amino acid sequences into latent-space embeddings, ready for use in diverse downstream tasks (DTs). By a common consensus, embeddings from the model's last layer are used, and the model's internal behavior remains poorly understood. We analyzed 13 PLMs across 15 DTs from 11 datasets to investigate the informativeness of embeddings created in intermediate PLM layers. We trained probe models on embeddings from each layer, compared their performance, and computed characteristics of the latent spaces they span to estimate the information they contain, and found that the last layers of PLMs rarely contained embeddings that led to the best results on downstream tasks. Furthermore, we identified a connection between DTs and the distribution across PLMs' layers of the relevant information to predict that task. For example, similarity between the pre-training objective and the objective of predicting properties of individual residues leads to a steady increase in understanding of such tasks across the layers of PLMs. On the other hand, for whole-protein tasks, we observe that the dataset, rather than the task itself, defines PLMs' ability to perform well on a DT. Embeddings from shallow layers of PLMs perform better for datasets that contain deep mutational scan (DMS) data, while datasets containing diverse natural proteins find most useful embeddings in the models' deeper layers. Additionally, we discover that the performance of PLMs drops significantly when tasks are introduced for artificial proteins.

card.problem: Protein language models (PLMs) are used as feature extractors: an amino-acid sequence is mapped to embeddings that feed downstream predictors. By convention the last-layer embedding is used, on the assumption that depth monotonically improves representations. Is that assumption right for self-supervised PLMs, and if not, what determines which layer carries the information a given downstream task needs?
card.setting: 13 PLMs from five model families across four architectures; 15 downstream tasks drawn from 11 datasets, spanning per-residue tasks (secondary structure, contacts) and whole-protein tasks (localization, solubility, stability, fluorescence, homology). Datasets split into deep-mutational-scan (DMS) type (many variants of one or few proteins) and diverse-natural-protein type. Includes artificial proteins (Rosetta-designed, ProGen-generated lysozymes). Analysis is layer-wise probing plus latent-space geometry.
card.method: For every PLM and every layer, train a probe model on that layer's embeddings for each downstream task and compare probe performance across layers. In parallel, compute geometric descriptors of each layer's latent space (intrinsic dimension, neighborhood overlap between consecutive layers) to characterize how representations evolve with depth. Relate the layer-vs- performance profile to (i) similarity between the masked-language-modeling pretraining objective and the downstream objective and (ii) dataset type. Repeat on artificial-protein tasks.
card.contribution: Systematic evidence that the last layer of a PLM is rarely the best layer for a downstream task. Identifies two determinants of where the useful information sits: objective mismatch (residue-level tasks, close to the MLM objective, improve monotonically with depth; whole-protein tasks do not) and dataset type (DMS datasets are best served by shallow layers, diverse-protein datasets by deep layers). Shows PLM performance drops sharply on artificial proteins even when they are verified functional, arguing PLMs accumulate an abstraction of naturally evolved sequence space, not of protein function per se.

mathematical_objects.name: linear classifier probe
mathematical_objects.role: Primary instrument: per-layer probe accuracy on a downstream task is the operational measure of how much task-relevant information that layer's embedding exposes.

mathematical_objects.name: intrinsic dimension
mathematical_objects.role: Geometric descriptor of each layer's latent space, used to characterize how the representation expands and contracts with depth independently of any label.

mathematical_objects.name: neighborhood overlap
mathematical_objects.role: Measures how much the local neighbor structure of a sequence is preserved between consecutive layers, tracking where representational change concentrates; used to show shallow and deep layers can resemble each other under MLM training.

mathematical_objects.name: masked language modeling
mathematical_objects.role: The pretraining objective whose (mis)alignment with a downstream objective is the paper's explanatory variable for the shape of the layer-vs- performance curve.

mathematical_objects.name: objective mismatch
mathematical_objects.role: The main explanatory construct: the larger the gap between the local token-level MLM objective and a global protein-level downstream objective, the earlier in the network the peak-performing layer sits and the more information is 'diluted' in deeper layers.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Conclusion: "The first factor is the difference between the pre-training and the downstream objectives. For residue-level tasks, the difference is lower than for protein-level ones, so PLMs tend to improve monotonically on such tasks."

mathematical_objects.name: k-nearest-neighbor density estimate
mathematical_objects.role: Cited and extended construct for judging embedding quality: an embedding's reliability is scored by the fraction of randomized non-biological sequences among its latent-space nearest neighbors — a k-NN-based out-of-distribution / density statistic — which the paper tracks across layers.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Intro: "They quantify the uncertainty of a protein embedding by the fraction of randomized non-biological sequences among its latent-space neighbors ... how does the distinction between natural and artificially designed proteins change across a network's layers?"

limitations: Findings are correlational: 'objective mismatch' and 'dataset type' are post-hoc groupings that co-vary (DMS datasets are both narrow and stability/fitness-oriented), and the paper does not disentangle them experimentally.
Probe performance conflates information content with linear accessibility; a deep layer could hold the information non-linearly and score worse.

The artificial-protein conclusion rests on two generation engines (Rosetta, ProGen lysozymes) and a small set of designed sequences; 'PLMs abstract evolved sequence space, not function' is a broad claim from a narrow sample.
Practical guidance ('use intermediate layers') depends on having a labelled validation set to pick the layer, which is the same data bottleneck that motivates using PLMs in the first place.
No single best layer generalizes; the result is a heterogeneity finding, so the actionable output is a procedure, not a recommendation.

title: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1's trunk-diffusion boundary
abstract: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors pair a representational trunk, which processes sequence and context, with a diffusion module, which generates atomic coordinates. How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure transfers essentially unchanged, whereas sequence chemistry is strongly attenuated. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model, intervening on the final trunk single representation that conditions the diffusion module. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently against matched-norm random controls, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive (F1 =0.82) produces no measurable increase in strand content: linear decodability does not imply causal influence at the site we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against sparse SwissProt annotations than against dense DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists. We release the trained trunk and diffusion SAEs, Boltz-1 per-residue activations, and the analysis code.

card.problem: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors have a representational trunk (processes sequence and evolutionary context) feeding a diffusion module (generates atomic coordinates). What biological information is present on each side of that architectural boundary, is that information actually used causally, and do standard interpretability evaluations measure it faithfully?
card.setting: Per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and the diffusion module of Boltz-1. Probing against dense secondary-structure labels (DSSP) and sparse curated annotations (SwissProt: signal peptides, disulfide bonds, amino-acid identity). Analysis tools: supervised linear probes, sparse autoencoders, and causal interventions on the final trunk single representation that conditions diffusion. Interventions are compared to matched-norm random directions. Trained SAEs, activations and code are released.
card.method: Train linear probes on activations from each module to test linear decodability of geometric and sequence-chemical features. Train sparse autoencoders on the same activations to extract candidate monosemantic features. Then intervene: add a probe-derived direction (helix, coil, strand) to the trunk's single representation with varying magnitude and measure the dose-dependent change in predicted structure against matched-norm random controls. Separately, re-score probes against sparse vs dense label sets to quantify how missing annotations inflate the apparent false-positive rate.
card.contribution: Shows the trunk keeps both geometry and sequence chemistry linearly decodable, while the diffusion module preserves geometry but strongly attenuates chemistry — evidence the two modules expose different information. Demonstrates that linear decodability does not imply causal influence: a strand direction with F1 = 0.82 produces no measurable change in strand content under intervention, whereas helix and coil directions steer structure dose-dependently. Shows scoring interpretability units against sparse annotations turns correct-but-unlabelled predictions into false positives, so such scores are lower bounds. Finds supervised probes beat single SAE features wherever a label exists.

mathematical_objects.name: linear probe
mathematical_objects.role: Primary measurement instrument: a linear map from per-residue activations to a biological label, whose accuracy is taken as a measure of how linearly accessible that concept is in a given module's representation.

mathematical_objects.name: sparse dictionary learning
mathematical_objects.role: Unsupervised decomposition of activations into an overcomplete set of sparsely-active features, used to search for monosemantic directions without labels; found less reliable than supervised probes for known concepts.

mathematical_objects.name: causal intervention
mathematical_objects.role: Tests whether a decodable direction is used: the direction is added to the trunk single representation and the resulting change in predicted structure is measured, isolating causal from merely correlational signal.

mathematical_objects.name: linear representation hypothesis
mathematical_objects.role: The organizing assumption: biological concepts correspond to directions in activation space that can be both read out by projection and written by addition; the paper's central finding is that readability and writability of a direction come apart.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract/intro: "test whether decodable directions can steer the model", "Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently against matched-norm random controls", "supervised probes ... provide more reliable steering directions" — concepts treated throughout as linear directions.

mathematical_objects.name: dose-response curve
mathematical_objects.role: The causal-effect readout: predicted secondary-structure content is plotted against intervention magnitude, and a monotone increase relative to matched-norm random controls is the evidence of causal influence.

mathematical_objects.name: evaluation under incomplete labels
mathematical_objects.role: Explains a systematic bias in interpretability metrics: when only some true positives are annotated, a correct prediction on an unannotated residue is scored as a false positive, so measured precision/F1 are lower bounds rather than estimates.
mathematical_objects.evidence: Abstract: "probes also score markedly lower against sparse SwissProt annotations than against dense DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds."

mathematical_objects.name: diffusion model
mathematical_objects.role: One of the two representational regimes analyzed: the coordinate- generating module whose per-residue activations retain geometry but lose sequence chemistry.

limitations: Interventions modify only the final trunk single representation s; the pair representation z is never touched, so the null result for the strand direction is confounded with 'strand information may live in z' — the paper acknowledges this but cannot resolve it.

Findings are for one model (Boltz-1); the trunk/diffusion contrast is plausibly architecture-specific and the paper's generalization claims to AlphaFold3-class models rest on concurrent work, not its own experiments.

Steering success is measured by change in the model's own predicted structure, not by physical plausibility or experimental structure, so 'inducible' means 'the predictor's output moves', not 'a real helix forms'.
Probe F1 and SAE feature scores against sparse labels are explicitly only lower bounds; the true decodability of sparsely-annotated features (signal peptides, disulfides) is not pinned down.
SAE-vs-probe comparison is restricted to concepts that already have labels, by construction; it says nothing about the setting where SAEs are supposed to help (unlabelled features).

title: On the completeness of several fortification-interdiction games in the Polynomial Hierarchy
abstract: Fortification-interdiction games are tri-level adversarial games where two opponents act in succession to protect, disrupt and simply use an infrastructure for a specific purpose. Many such games have been formulated and tackled in the literature through specific algorithmic methods, however very few investigations exist on the completeness of such fortification problems in order to locate them rigorously in the polynomial hierarchy. We clarify the completeness status of several well-known fortification problems, such as the Tri-level Interdiction Knapsack Problem with unit fortification and attack weights, the Max-flow Interdiction Problem and Shortest Path Interdiction Problem with Fortification, the Multi-level Critical Node Problem with unit weights, as well as a well-studied electric grid defence planning problem. For all of these problems, we prove their completeness either for the $\Sigma^p_2$ or the $\Sigma^p_3$ class of the polynomial hierarchy. We also prove that the Multi-level Fortification-Interdiction Knapsack Problem with an arbitrary number of protection and interdiction rounds and unit fortification and attack weights is complete for any level of the polynomial hierarchy, therefore providing a useful basis for further attempts at proving the completeness of protection-interdiction games at any level of said hierarchy.

card.problem: Tri-level fortification-interdiction games (a defender fortifies, an attacker interdicts, a user then operates the infrastructure) are solved in the literature by ad hoc decomposition methods, but their exact position in the polynomial hierarchy is largely unknown. Where do the standard fortification problems sit, and can that be pinned down even in the commonly used unit-cost regime?
card.setting: Discrete tri-level (and multi-level) combinatorial optimization: knapsack, max-flow, shortest-path, critical-node, and an electric-grid defence problem, each in a Defender-Attacker-Defender form. Emphasis on the unit fortification / unit attack weight case, where budget constraints become cardinality constraints. Worst-case computational complexity, no probabilistic or average-case component.
card.method: Polynomial-time many-one reductions from canonical quantified problems (quantified Boolean / quantified combinatorial problems complete for Sigma^p_2 and Sigma^p_3, and generalized quantified knapsack for arbitrary levels) to each fortification problem, matched with membership arguments placing the problem in the same class. A multi-round interdiction knapsack with arbitrary lower-level weights and profits is used as a structural gadget to lift completeness to any level of the hierarchy.
card.contribution: Establishes Sigma^p_2-completeness of the max-flow interdiction with fortification, the shortest-path interdiction with fortification, and an electric-grid fortification problem (unit fortification costs); Sigma^p_3-completeness of the multi-level critical-node problem with unit weights and profits, refining a prior tree-case result; and completeness for every level of the polynomial hierarchy of the multi-round interdiction knapsack with unit fortification and attack costs, giving a reusable base problem for future hardness proofs of protection-interdiction games.

mathematical_objects.name: Polynomial hierarchy
mathematical_objects.role: The complexity scale on which every result is stated; the paper locates each fortification problem at a specific level and, for the multi-round knapsack, at every level simultaneously.

mathematical_objects.name: Many-one reduction
mathematical_objects.role: The proof instrument: each hardness claim is a polynomial reduction from a known complete problem for the target class into the fortification problem.

mathematical_objects.name: Multilevel / tri-level optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The problem structure under study; the nesting of min/max quantifiers over successive players is exactly what forces the problems above NP.

mathematical_objects.name: Network interdiction problem
mathematical_objects.role: The inner two levels (attacker plus user) for the graph-based instances; their polynomial or NP-hard lower level determines the base level from which fortification adds one quantifier.

mathematical_objects.name: Fortification
mathematical_objects.role: The outermost decision layer that makes chosen elements immune to attack; adding it is the operation whose complexity cost the paper measures.

mathematical_objects.name: Knapsack problem
mathematical_objects.role: The structure-poor base problem used as a gadget; arbitrary lower-level weights and profits let the reduction be iterated to reach any hierarchy level.

mathematical_objects.name: Critical node problem
mathematical_objects.role: Graph-fragmentation problem whose fortified multi-level version is shown Sigma^p_3-complete even with unit weights, sharpening the known weighted/tree case.

limitations: Results are worst-case hardness classifications; they say nothing about instances met in practice or about the performance of the decomposition algorithms currently used.

Membership arguments are sketched in the extracted text but the full proofs (and the precise quantified base problems) are in sections not extracted; the exact reduction gadgets are not verifiable from abstract/intro/conclusion alone.
Several completeness results are specifically for the unit-cost regime; the conclusion notes the general-cost SPIPF and TEPGFP cases remain open.
For the multi-level knapsack the 'any level' result needs an arbitrary number of fortification-interdiction rounds; with a fixed small number of rounds the picture is only partly resolved.

title: Queueing models with random resetting
abstract: We introduce and study some queueing models with random resetting, including Markovian and non--Markovian models under the first-come first-served (FCFS) discipline. The Markovian models include M/M/$r$ and M/M/1+M queues with random resetting, in which a continuous-time Markov chain is formulated, with transitions including a resetting to state zero in addition to arrivals and services. We explicitly characterize the stationary distributions of the queueing processes in these models by using parting balance equations. We derive expressions for standard performance measures such as the delay probability, expected queue length and waiting time, as well as probability of a customer completing service before resetting in the M/M/$r$ model, and probability of abandonment before service or resetting in the M/M/1+M model. The non--Markovian models include GI/GI/1, GI/GI/$r$ and GI/GI/$\infty$ queues with random resetting to state zero at arrival times. For GI/GI/1 and GI/GI/$r$ queues under the FCFS discipline, we introduce modified Lindley and Kiefer--Wolfowitz recursions, respectively. Using an operator representation for these recursions, we characterize the stationary distributions via convergent series, as solutions to the modified Wiener--Hopf equations. For GI/GI/$\infty$ queues with resettings, we utilize a version of the Kiefer--Wolfowitz recursion, and also characterize the corresponding stationary distribution.

card.problem: How can the stationary distributions and standard performance measures of queueing systems that clear (reset to the empty state) at random times be characterized explicitly, for both Markovian and non-Markovian service and arrival processes?
card.setting: FCFS discipline throughout. Markovian models: M/M/r and M/M/1+M queues with a resetting transition to state 0 added to the birth-death dynamics, giving a continuous-time Markov chain that is no longer a birth-death process. Non-Markovian models: GI/GI/1, GI/GI/r and GI/GI/infinity queues with resetting to zero at arrival epochs.
card.method: For the CTMC models, partial balance equations are solved to give the stationary law as an integral representation plus a terminating generalized hypergeometric sum, the two pieces obeying the same recursion with different boundary conditions. For GI/GI/1 and GI/GI/r, modified Lindley and Kiefer-Wolfowitz recursions are introduced and written in operator form, from which the stationary distribution is expressed as a convergent series solving a modified Wiener-Hopf equation. For GI/GI/infinity, an adapted Kiefer-Wolfowitz recursion on the vector of elapsed service times is used.
card.contribution: Explicit stationary distributions for the M/M/r queue with resetting for general r (new) and for the M/M/1+M queue with resetting (new); a proof that resetting makes the queueing CTMC positive recurrent for any traffic intensity, even zero service rate; a unified operator/series characterization for GI/GI/1 and GI/GI/r with resetting that holds whether or not the underlying queue is stable; and an explicit stationary law for GI/GI/infinity with resetting.

mathematical_objects.name: Continuous-time Markov chain
aliases: birth-death process with an added jump to zero
mathematical_objects.role: The state process for the Markovian models; adding the resetting transition breaks the birth-death structure but keeps an explicitly solvable stationary law.

mathematical_objects.name: Partial balance equations
mathematical_objects.role: The tool used to guess and verify the stationary distribution of the resetting CTMC without a birth-death product form.

mathematical_objects.name: Lindley recursion
mathematical_objects.role: The waiting-time recursion for GI/GI/1; its modified version incorporates resetting at arrival epochs.

mathematical_objects.name: Kiefer-Wolfowitz recursion
mathematical_objects.role: The multi-server workload-vector recursion for GI/GI/r and, adapted, for GI/GI/infinity; modified to include resetting.

mathematical_objects.name: Wiener-Hopf equation
mathematical_objects.role: Characterizes the stationary waiting-time law; the resetting models satisfy a modified Wiener-Hopf equation solved by a convergent operator series.

mathematical_objects.name: Stochastic resetting
mathematical_objects.role: The mechanism under study: instantaneous return of the system to the empty state at random (here Poisson or arrival-triggered) times.

mathematical_objects.name: Positive recurrence / stationary distribution
mathematical_objects.role: The property established unconditionally under resetting, in contrast to the traffic-intensity-below-one requirement for standard queues.

limitations: Resetting is restricted to the empty state, and in the non-Markovian case to arrival epochs.
Heavy-traffic diffusion approximations of reset queues are not treated.
Some stationary laws are given as convergent series that may not be numerically transparent.
No transient analysis for general r.

title: Properties of Turnpike Functions for Discounted Finite Markov Decision Processes
abstract: This paper studies convergence times of the Value Iteration Algorithm (VIA) for discounted discrete-time Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with finite state and action sets. For each discount factor, starting from a finite number of iterations, which is called the turnpike integer, the VIA generates deterministic optimal policies for infinite-horizon problems. Turnpike integers are viewed as functions of discount factors called turnpike functions. We design an algorithm to detect in strongly polynomial time whether a discount factor is irregular - at which the sets of optimal policies change. We then prove that a turnpike function is upper-semicontinuous and finitely-piecewise constant on any closed subinterval of [0,1) that does not contain irregular points. In particular, we prove that for small discount factors a turnpike function is bounded by the number of states and design an algorithm based on the VIA to solve an MDP for all small discount factors in strongly polynomial time.

card.problem: For a discounted finite Markov decision process, value iteration eventually starts producing only optimal policies after some number of iterations, the turnpike integer. As a function of the discount factor this turnpike function governs the true complexity of value iteration, yet its structure (continuity, boundedness, piecewise behavior) near the discount factors where the optimal policy set changes is only partly understood. What are its properties, and can the problematic discount factors be detected efficiently?
card.setting: Discrete-time MDPs with finite state and action sets, infinite-horizon expected total discounted reward, discount factor alpha in [0,1). Terminal rewards are not assumed zero (a generalization over prior work). Analysis is exact and combinatorial; complexity is measured as strongly polynomial (arithmetic-operation count independent of the magnitude of the data).
card.method: Classify discount factors as regular or irregular (break points and touching points) via comparisons of finite-step transition probabilities between deterministic policies, which can be done in strongly polynomial time. On intervals free of irregular points, analyze the turnpike function using the analyticity of value functions there, proving upper semicontinuity and a boundedness/finite-partition equivalence. For small discount factors, bound the turnpike function by the number of states and build a value-iteration-based strongly polynomial solver valid for all sufficiently small alpha.
card.contribution: A strongly polynomial algorithm to test whether a discount factor is irregular; a proof that the turnpike function is upper semicontinuous on each partition interval and that an interval splits into finitely many constant (turnpike) subintervals if and only if the turnpike function is bounded there; sufficient conditions for boundedness near irregular points (with a counterexample showing the known necessary conditions are not sufficient); and a proof that for small discount factors the turnpike function is bounded by the number of states, giving a strongly polynomial value-iteration solver for all small discount factors.

mathematical_objects.name: Markov decision process
mathematical_objects.role: The object being solved; finiteness of state and action sets is the standing assumption under which every result holds.

mathematical_objects.name: Value iteration algorithm
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithm whose convergence time is the subject; the turnpike function is precisely the iteration count past which it emits only optimal policies.

mathematical_objects.name: Turnpike function
mathematical_objects.role: The central object: the map from discount factor to the number of value iterations needed before all generated policies are optimal.

mathematical_objects.name: Discount factor
mathematical_objects.role: The parameter over which the turnpike function is studied; its classification into regular and irregular points organizes the whole analysis.

mathematical_objects.name: Strongly polynomial algorithm
mathematical_objects.role: The complexity standard for the detection algorithm and the small-discount solver; contrasts with value iteration, which is only weakly polynomial.

mathematical_objects.name: Blackwell optimality
mathematical_objects.role: Characterizes optimal policies for discount factors near 1 (above the largest break point); invoked in framing the open problem of solving for all alpha.

mathematical_objects.name: Upper semicontinuity
mathematical_objects.role: The regularity proved for the turnpike function on irregular-point-free intervals; the piecewise-constant structure is what makes turnpike intervals well defined.

mathematical_objects.name: Optimal policy set
mathematical_objects.role: Constant on each partition interval; irregular points are exactly where it changes, which is why the turnpike function can jump there.

limitations: Everything depends on finiteness of both state and action sets; the conclusion states that for infinite state or action sets optimal policies may not exist and the turnpike integer can be infinite, so the theory does not extend as stated.
The sufficient conditions for boundedness near an irregular point are not shown to be necessary; a full characterization of boundedness is not obtained.

The strongly polynomial solver is proved only for 'small' discount factors below an explicit threshold; solving efficiently for discount factors in an arbitrary interval, or near 1, is left as an open direction.
Proofs and the exact algorithm statements are in sections not extracted; the card relies on the abstract, introduction and conclusion summaries.

title: A Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Estimation Method for High Dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models
abstract: Estimating high dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models presents severe computational challenges. Traditional simultaneous estimators frequently suffer from numerical instability and prohibitive computational costs. Moreover, there are no tractable algorithms for families such as Poisson, negative binomial, and gamma. To overcome these limitations, this article introduces a Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Expectation-Maximization framework. The proposed method isolates the structural model from the measurement model. First, it approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observed indicators. Second, it employs marginal quasi-likelihood estimating equations to evaluate the structural parameters, deriving the necessary conditional moments either exactly or through Monte Carlo integration. This approach completely avoids the need to evaluate the full joint likelihood. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our method drastically reduces computational runtime, providing a numerically stable framework that minimizes the mean squared error and structural bias to yield a scalable and flexible solution for analyzing complex latent variable models.

card.problem: Estimating high-dimensional generalized structural equation models (equivalently generalized linear latent variable models) is computationally hard: the observed-data likelihood is a p-dimensional integral over the latent space, full-information maximum likelihood is intractable for discrete indicators, and there is no practical algorithm for outcome families such as Poisson, negative binomial, or gamma. How can the structural regression coefficients be estimated at scale, stably, for arbitrary GLM outcome families?
card.setting: n independent subjects; a p-vector of latent predictors eta ~ N(0, Phi) measured by a J-vector of mixed binary/ordinal/continuous indicators through a linear factor measurement model Z = nu + Lambda eta + epsilon; an outcome y whose conditional mean given eta follows a GLM (or quasi-likelihood family) with link g and structural coefficient vector beta. High-dimensional latent space is the regime of interest. Frequentist estimation; evaluation by Monte Carlo simulation plus a Big Five Inventory application with ordinal indicators. No asymptotic theory presented in the available sections.
card.method: Two-Stage Quasi-Likelihood EM (TSQLEM), a limited-information estimator that separates the measurement model from the structural model. Stage 1 approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observed indicators, eta | Z. Stage 2 derives the conditional first and second moments of the outcome given the indicators, y | Z, either in closed form or by Monte Carlo integration, and plugs them into marginal quasi-score estimating equations for the structural parameters, solved by iteratively reweighted least squares. The full joint likelihood is never evaluated.
card.contribution: Introduces the TSQLEM framework: by decoupling the measurement model from the structural model and estimating the structural coefficients from marginal quasi-score equations built on conditional moments of y | Z, it makes high-dimensional GSEM estimation numerically stable and fast, and extends tractable estimation to quasi-likelihood outcome families (Poisson, negative binomial, gamma) that lack existing algorithms. Simulations report large runtime reductions and lower MSE / structural bias relative to full- and limited-information competitors.

limitations: No methods or conclusion section was available; the exact stage-1 approximation of eta | Z, the form of the quasi-score equations, and the treatment of the factor loadings/thresholds are not visible.

No theoretical properties are stated in the extracted text — no consistency, no asymptotic variance, no standard-error construction for the two-stage estimator (a known difficulty for sequential estimators, where stage-1 uncertainty must propagate).

Two-stage / limited-information estimators are generally less efficient than FIML when the model is correctly specified; the extracted text frames this only as a robustness benefit and does not quantify the efficiency loss.
Stage 1 relies on a Gaussian latent structure and a linear factor measurement model; robustness to non-normal latent variables or nonlinear measurement is not discussed.

'High-dimensional' refers to the latent dimension p; there is no explicit sparsity or regularization on Phi, Lambda, or beta in the available text, so the high-dimensional regime's statistical (as opposed to computational) challenges are unaddressed.
Empirical validation is simulations plus one psychometric dataset (Big Five); generalization across indicator types and outcome families is asserted, not demonstrated in the extract.
